theme: The census, God’s ordered people prepared for the journey
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 1:1-2:34. A new book begins, and it opens with a census and a camp plan. The text is full of numbers, so read it for the pattern and not for the arithmetic. Ask what it says about how God organizes and cares for his people.
settingTheScene: Israel has been at Mount Sinai for almost a year. The covenant has been made, the tabernacle built, and the laws of Leviticus given. Now, on the first day of the second month of the second year, God tells Moses to count the fighting men and to arrange the camp. Numbers takes its English name from these censuses, though the Hebrew title is “In the wilderness.” The book tells how a redeemed people travel from Sinai toward the land God promised, and how a whole generation fails to enter it.
observation: God commands Moses to number “all the congregation of the people of Israel, by clans, by fathers” houses’ (1:2).
Each tribe has a named leader who helps with the count (1:5-16).
The total of men twenty years old and up, able to go to war, is 603,550 (1:46).
The Levites are not counted with the rest, because they are to care for the tabernacle (1:47-53).
The tribes camp around the tabernacle, three on each side, “each by his own banner” (2:2).
Judah camps on the east, the side of the entrance, and leads out first (2:3, 9).
The tabernacle and the Levites are at the center of the camp (2:17).
“Thus did the people of Israel. According to all that the LORD commanded Moses, so they camped by their standards, and so they set out” (2:34).
interpretation:
A census may seem a dull way to begin a book, but it says something important. God knows his people by name and by family. Each tribe has a leader. Each man is counted. In a world where slaves were nameless, Israel is a people whose members are known. The counting recalls the promise to Abraham of descendants like the stars, now visibly coming true in a host of hundreds of thousands.

The census is also a military preparation. Israel is about to march toward a land that other nations hold. The numbers are meant to give confidence, and they also bring responsibility, since each man counted is accountable to serve. But this army is not led by generals. It follows the tabernacle, and the cloud.

The camp plan is a picture in space. The tabernacle sits in the center, and twelve tribes surround it in four groups of three. God does not dwell at the edge. He is the center, and all of life is arranged around him. The Levites camp between the tabernacle and the people, a protective ring that reflects the holiness you read about in Leviticus. Everyone has a place, and no one is left out.

Notice the repeated phrase, “as the LORD commanded Moses.” The book begins with obedience. It is the high point before the failure that follows. For a moment, Israel is exactly what God designed: a people in order, near their God, ready to move. The tragedy of the rest of Numbers is that this orderly people will not trust the God who has arranged them.

For us, the lesson is simple. God does not scatter his people. He gathers them around himself and gives each a place and a task.
connection: The church is described in the same terms. Paul says that God arranged the members of the body “as he chose” (1 Corinthians 12:18), and Ephesians 4:16 speaks of the whole body “joined and held together.” Hebrews 12:23 speaks of “the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven,” and Jesus told his disciples to rejoice that their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20). Revelation 21:12-14 pictures the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles around the new Jerusalem.
application:
Thank God that he knows you by name, and that you are counted among his people.

Ask where your place is in the body of Christ, and whether you are filling it.

Notice the centrality of the tabernacle in Israel’s camp, and ask what is at the center of your life.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he knows his people by name and that you are counted among them.
Ask him to put you where he wants you in his body.
Ask him to keep himself at the center of your life.
